https://www.katc.com/us-news/crime/socia.text: Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested Saturday in Miami after U.K. prosecutors said they brought further rape and sex trafficking charges against them.Britain's Crown Prosecution Service said the new charges relate to four further victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The charges include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.”The charges announced Saturday, which bring the total number of alleged victims in the U.K. to seven, are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the brothers that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have denied wrongdoing.Here are some things to know about the Tate brothers:Who the Tate Brothers areAndrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, are dual U.S.-British citizens known for their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny.Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist who has amassed more than 10 million followers, most of them boys and young men, on X. He has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines.He also runs an online academy where he says he teaches young men how to get rich and attract women. Tristan Tate is also a former kickboxer.The brothers are avid supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump.What the Tates are charged withAndrew Tate and his brother have faced multiple charges in the U.K. and Romania, where they moved to in 2016.British prosecutors said the new charges relate to alleged offenses that took place between 2010 and 2017. They said Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault and 19 charges for offenses relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.FROM THE ARCHIVES | Police raid Andrew Tate's home in Romania as new allegations involving minors emergeTristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking.The Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement it “has requested the extradition of the Tates from the U.S. They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the U.K.”The Tates already face previous charges of rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015.In June, a U.K. High Court judge threw out a legal bid by the Tates to be told the names of their accusers.In Romania, the siblings were arrested in late 2022 along with two Romanian women. The four were accused of participating in criminal schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems.The case hasn’t been closed, and there is also a separate legal case against the brothers in Romania.Andrew Tate has repeatedly claimed that prosecutors in Romania have no evidence against him and that there is a political conspiracy to silence him.Why the Tates were in the U.S.British police previously sought the Tates' extradition to the U.K. once their legal proceedings in Romania concluded.But in February 2025 they were allowed to leave Romania after authorities lifted travel restrictions, and they flew to Florida on a private jet.Romania's foreign minister said at the time that a U.S. official in the Trump administration had expressed interest in the brothers’ legal case in Romania.Trump said he knew “nothing about” the case when asked if his administration pressured the Romania government to release the Tates.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: China's C919 takes off on a test flight in Shanghai in July. The passenger jet built by Comac is scheduled to make its first international flight on Wednesday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images View image in fullscreen China's C919 takes off on a test flight in Shanghai in July. The passenger jet built by Comac is scheduled to make its first international flight on Wednesday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images China Passenger jet billed as China’s answer to Boeing and Airbus prepares to make first international flight The Comac C919 will fly from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, although experts say it could take generations for it to challenge the west’s dominance of the industry Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent Tue 11 Aug 2026 22.02 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 22.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google China hopes to break into the world of commercial aviation with the first international flight of a Chinese-made passenger jet scheduled for Wednesday. The Comac C919 will take off from Beijing capital international airport at 3pm, landing in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, just over two hours later. It has been billed as China’s alternative to the Boeing-Airbus duopoly that dominates global aviation, particularly in Asia, but analysts say it could take generations before a Chinese aircraft could meaningfully challenge their global dominance. The C919 is made by the Chinese state-owned aircraft manufacturer Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) and is similar in size to the Boeing 737. Chinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutiny Read more The C919 has been flying on domestic routes operated by Chinese airlines since 2023. But Wednesday’s Air China flight to Ulaanbaatar will be the first time that the narrow-body jet is used on a commercial international route. “This is essentially a public relations move,” said Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. “Ulaanbaatar was likely chosen because of how close it is to Beijing. It doesn’t change the fact that the plane was years overdue, is composed of western components, and is less efficient than its Boeing and Airbus cousins.” China has long dreamed of building its own jet. When the C919 was unveiled in 2015 , Li Jiaxiang, the head of China’s civil aviation authority, said: “A great nation must have its own large commercial aircraft.” But progress has been slow, even while China has whizzed ahead in other hi-tech fields, such as robotics and electric vehicles (EVs). That is because aviation requires the integration of many different types of advanced science and engineering, as well as parts sourced from overseas. An analysis by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in 2020 found that more than half of the C919’s suppliers were in the US. View image in fullscreen China’s C919, its first self-developed large passenger jetliner, is unveiled in Shanghai in November 2015. Photograph: ChinaFotoPress/Getty Images “Large passenger aircraft and jet engines are extremely complex and challenging to manufacture. They require precision components, complex electro-mechanical control systems, and the ability to coordinate a vast global supply chain,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at Brookings focused on China’s industrial policy. “There’s a reason there are basically only two major commercial aircraft makers in the world. Building large passenger jets that are safe and reliable is an order of magnitude more difficult than making EVs,” Chan said. Last year Comac reportedly delivered only 15 units of the C919 to customers, well short of its target of 75. Comac did not respond to a request for comment. Comac primarily serves Chinese domestic airlines. In 2023, the Brunei-based airline GallopAir signed a $2bn deal to purchase 30 planes from Comac, including 15 of the C919, but the airline is not operating commercially yet. The C919 has not been approved by European or American regulators. Last year the US reportedly suspended the export of some products to Comac for use in the C919 jet amid the tit-for-tat restrictions that Beijing and Washington used against each other during the US-China trade war. The two countries later agreed a trade war truce that is set to expire in November. When US president Donald Trump visited Beijing in May for a state visit , one of the few takeaways from the trip was an agreement from China to buy 200 jets from Boeing. In return, the US provided supply guarantees for aircraft engine parts and components for its own manufacturing. China sees being able to build its own commercial aircraft as a national security priority. In a recent interview with Chinese state media, Zhang Yanzhong, an academic of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a leading aviation expert who worked on the C919, said reliance on other countries for large aircraft technology would “threaten national strategic security”. However, there was still “a long way to go before achieving commercial success”, Zhang said. Experts have pointed out that Comac’s dependence on foreign suppliers goes beyond the supply of individual components. International suppliers have also provided guidance about how to integrate complex components and software together into sky-worthy commercial aircraft. Kennedy argued it was misleading to describe the C919 as a Chinese plane because so many of its parts were imported. He said it was “very unlikely” for Comac to become a serious challenger to Boeing and Airbus, “even a generation from now”. Chan said Comac could still face “a long road to gaining trust among airlines and passengers”. Zhang called on China’s young engineers to contribute their talents to China’s aviation ambitions, saying: “Though the journey may be fraught with difficulties, a fledgling eagle can soar faster than its parent.” Explore more on these topics China Asia Pacific Air transport news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/08/.text: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav German police disarmed a drone carrying explosives after it was discovered near Ukrainian cargo aircraft parked at Leipzig airport—and authorities are looking into the possibility of a second drone after an approaching aircraft collided with something midair. The drone, first spotted by an airport employee, was hovering close to the ground between two parked An-124 cargo aircraft owned by Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines shortly before midnight on August 4, according to The Guardian . It had apparently been modified to help avoid detection by the airport’s drone defense sensors, said Alexander Dobrindt, federal minister of the interior for Germany, during a press conference. Dobrindt described the drone as carrying a fist-sized package of a substance believed to be the plastic explosive Semtex. Only a failed detonator prevented the drone from exploding near the Ukrainian cargo aircraft, he said. A bus driver managed to kick the flying drone and caused it to crash, according to Detlef Seif, a lawmaker and member of the German parliament’s interior committee. In an interview with Reuters , Seif described the driver’s actions as “very daring and courageous, but also very dangerous,” while acknowledging that “it is possible that his intervention prevented the intended attack.” German police used a bomb disposal robot to help disarm the drone and later carried out a controlled explosion, according to BBC News . Contrary to some media reports, the German Interior Ministry has denied that the apparently targeted Ukrainian cargo aircraft were carrying weapons or other munitions for delivery to Ukraine, according to Deutsche Welle . Instead, government officials described the aircraft as having been empty at the time of the drone incident. The incident forced Leipzig/Halle airport—one of Europe’s largest air cargo hubs—to close to all air traffic for several hours. That forced 19 flights to divert away from the airport , including a Boeing 757 operated by the shipping company DHL that was forced to abort its landing approach, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24. As the DHL-operated aircraft started climbing again, it collided with another flying object midair and diverted to land at Hanover airport with minor damage, German police reported in a statement . German authorities are looking into the possibility that the object was a second drone. The possible culprit and motive German officials have not officially named a suspect behind the attempted attack but have opened a counterterrorism investigation. Dobrindt acknowledged that “we are dealing with a contest here that possibly involves foreign powers,” and described the incident as a “hybrid threat scenario.” The incident has already spurred Roderich Kiesewetter, a lawmaker and member of the German parliament’s intelligence committee, to more directly describe Russia as being responsible for the “attempted act of terrorism.” As a major hub for air cargo, Leipzig/Halle airport frequently oversees the transit of shipments for NATO and the German military. It is also the current home base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines, which operates a charter cargo service fleet that includes the world’s largest operational cargo aircraft, the Antonov An-124 Ruslan. The incident also evoked a potentially telling reaction from Alexander Sosnowski, a pro-Kremlin propagandist who regularly appears as a guest on Russian state television. In a short video posted on Telegram, Sosnowski clearly assumed the attempted attack was a Russian operation targeting the Ukrainian aircraft and expressed disappointment that it had failed, according to The Bild , a German tabloid newspaper. Repeated drone incursions and missing defenses These latest incidents follow dozens of drone sightings over other European airports, along with military bases, ports, and energy and industrial facilities, since 2024. In May, Munich airport in Germany closed twice within 24 hours following possible drone sightings. Drone incursions have become especially more frequent in Northern and Eastern Europe, given their closer proximity to Russia and the ongoing war in Ukraine. Those incursions have forced fighter jets to scramble repeatedly in response and have led to a building fire and injuries in Romania following a Russian drone crash. But the long-promised European Drone Defence Initiative that was supposed to create the equivalent of a “drone wall” to provide counter-drone surveillance and defenses has yet to materialize in any meaningful way, said Ulrike Franke , a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, in an article for World Politics Review . Instead, individual European countries such as Poland have been building their own national counter-drone systems. Germany has already provided about $118 billion to support Ukraine since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to Deutsche Welle . Beyond supplying weapons and humanitarian aid, Germany has also trained more than 24,000 Ukrainian soldiers and is hosting more than 1 million Ukrainian refugees. Some of Germany’s latest cooperative ventures with Ukraine have involved joint production of new military drones. Ars recently covered a $100 million deal—reportedly funded by Germany—that is equipping the Ukrainian military with drones capable of performing AI target tracking . This story was updated on August 7, 2026 to include details on the bus driver credited with taking down the drone. Jeremy Hsu Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu is a reporter exploring a wide range of topics across deep tech and AI. He has previously written for New Scientist, Scientific American, IEEE Spectrum, Wired, Undark Magazine and MIT Tech Review, among many other publications, about topics such as deepfakes, data centers, drones, battery tech, robotics, and GPS jamming. He also has a Master of Arts in Journalism from NYU, and a bachelor's degree from University of Pennsylvania in History and Sociology of Science, with a minor in English. 163 Comments Comments Forum view Loading comments... https://www.thezimbabwean.co/2026/09/evi.text: Holding power does not make someone immune to mental health issues. Tendai Ruben Mbofana When political discourse touches on the psychological state of those in high office, a curious double standard often emerges. To directly receive my articles please join my WhatsApp Channel on: https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VaqprWCIyPtRnKpkHe08 If an ordinary citizen walks into a public square declaring themselves a divine monarch, demanding that neighbors bow to their supreme authority, society rightly identifies a mental health crisis requiring professional intervention. Yet, when a head of state orchestrates the exact same theater from a presidential palace, a starkly different reaction takes hold. As they demand veneration, manufacture ancient royal lineages, and organize grand rituals to bestow titles of transcendent glory upon themselves, the world far too often dismisses it as mere political strategy or eccentric posturing. It is time to strip away the protective veneer of statecraft and confront a uncomfortable reality. When political leaders exhibit an unquenchable thirst for deification and grandiosity, they are not merely playing tough politics. They are displaying textbook signs of deep-seated psychological instability. Throughout human history, the pursuit of total control has frequently crossed the line from ruthless ambition into severe personality pathology. Psychiatrists and political psychologists have long documented how unchecked authority acts as a catalyst for underlying mental health disorders, particularly malignant narcissism, severe paranoia, and megalomania. Leaders consumed by delusions of grandeur demonstrate a profound detachment from reality. They surround themselves with sycophants who validate their inflated self-image, systematically dismantling any institution or individual that dares to offer a reality check. Consider the historical trail of devastation left by rulers who succumbed to these psychological defects. When Jean-Bédel Bokassa bankrupted the Central African Republic to stage a lavish coronation crowning himself emperor, it was not a rational strategy for national governance—it was the unhinged manifestation of pathological grandiosity. When Saparmurat Niyazov renamed the months of the calendar after himself and erected a rotating gold statue in Turkmenistan, or when Idi Amin declared himself the “Uncrowned King of Scotland” while his nation fractured, these were not the actions of stable minds navigating statecraft. Equally unhinged was Mobutu Sese Seko, who built a multi-million-dollar marble palace complex in the jungle and forced state television to display his face descending from the clouds as a deity every evening before the news. In Iraq, Saddam Hussein commissioned grand monuments featuring giant casts of his own hands and ordered a Quran written in his own blood to cement his status as a sacred figure. Across history, the pattern repeats: from Caligula declaring himself a living god in Rome to Nicolae Ceaușescu destroying historic Bucharest to build a monumental presidential palace for his personal glorification. These are not isolated eccentricities of leadership. They were the outward symptoms of a mind consumed by megalomania, where the leader’s internal fantasy completely eclipses the living reality of the people they govern. According to established scientific research, the hallmark of this mental instability is a dangerous cognitive dissonance. A leader suffering from grandiose delusions genuinely begins to believe in their own myth. They view themselves not as temporary public servants bound by constitutions, but as destined figures, sacred rulers, or reincarnations of historic empires. In their mind, their personal survival and ego become synonymous with the survival of the state itself. Consequently, any dissent is no longer viewed as legitimate political opposition, but as treason against the cosmos. This detachment from basic reality carries catastrophic consequences for ordinary citizens. When a ruler’s mental health is dominated by grandiose narcissism, their decision-making becomes entirely distorted. National budgets are squandered on monuments, palaces, and vanity projects designed to soothe an insatiable ego, while public infrastructure collapses, poverty deepens, and basic services vanish. The leader’s clinical lack of empathy allows them to ignore the suffering of millions, viewing the population not as human beings with rights, but as props in a grand personal performance. Worse still, grandiosity rarely exists in a vacuum; it is almost always paired with acute paranoia. Because the grandiose leader’s self-image is fundamentally fragile, any refusal by the public or political peers to endorse their divine status triggers intense rage and fear. To protect the delusion, the ruler turns to purges, systemic fear, and arbitrary cruelty. The quest to be worshiped as a king or living deity invariably ends in a nightmare of repression for the nation forced to endure it. Recognizing these behaviors as symptoms of mental instability is not an academic exercise; it is a matter of national survival. Society must stop treating extreme political grandiosity as a normal feature of authoritarian rule. When leaders begin mapping out personal mythologies, seeking royal crowns, or framing their authority as infinite and permanent, it is a urgent signal that power has corrupted their psychological stability. True strength in leadership is defined by humility, emotional maturity, constitutional discipline, and a grounded commitment to human dignity. The moment a leader demands to be elevated above reality itself, they demonstrate an undeniable truth. Those who believe they are born to rule as gods or kings are, in truth, the most psychologically unfit to rule at all. Tendai Ruben Mbofana is a social justice advocate and writer. http://www.shanghainews.net/news/2793828.text: Home China News International News Business News Search News Network China's Uyghur crackdown under scrutiny as forced labour, cultural erasure, transnational repression draw concern ANI 18 Oct 2026, 17:36 GMT+ Munich [Germany], October 18 (ANI): The World Uyghur Congress (WUC) has released its weekly brief highlighting China's forced labour, environmental damage, cultural assimilation and restrictions on human rights advocacy in East Turkistan. An investigation by the Outlaw Ocean Project, published in The Globe and Mail on October 9, examined China's expanding aquaculture industry in the Taklamakan Desert. While Chinese authorities promote desert fish farming as a technological breakthrough, the report highlighted allegations of state-backed forced labour, coerced relocations and land seizures involving Uyghurs and other Turkic groups. It also raised environmental concerns over river and lake pollution and the extensive use of antibiotics and chemicals. Seafood processed in the region reportedly continues to reach markets in North America and Europe through international supply chains, raising questions about compliance with import restrictions, including the United States' Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. On October 12, the WUC expressed concern over Nobel Peace Prize recognition for Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, citing her tenure as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. The organisation alleged that information identifying Uyghur and other Chinese human rights defenders was shared with Beijing during that period. Former WUC president Dolkun Isa reportedly faced obstacles in securing accreditation and accessing the UN Human Rights Council between 2012 and 2013. The WUC argued that Uyghur activists were inadequately protected during Pillay's tenure. Meanwhile, WUC President Turgunjan Alawdun and Uyghur Centre for Democracy and Human Rights (UZDM) President Dolkun Isa attended Forum 2000 in Prague, meeting European political figures to highlight alleged abuses in East Turkistan. In Warsaw, the organisations also discussed transnational repression at the OSCE Warsaw Human Dimension Conference and how democracies can better protect communities targeted across borders. Separately, Asia Sentinel published an article on October 13 examining the alleged suppression of the Uyghur language and cultural identity. Uyghur poet and rights advocate Abduweli Ayup is scheduled to present research at Sorbonne University in Paris on October 24. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: Președintele Nicușor Dan participă vineri, de la ora 12:00, la reuniunea informală a Consiliului European, organizată la Dublin, unde liderii europeni vor discuta despre dezvoltarea inteligenței artificiale și poziția UE în competiția globală din acest domeniu. Pe agenda întâlnirii se află și propunerea premierului italian Giorgia Meloni privind transmiterea unui mesaj coordonat al Uniunii Europene în negocierile de pace pentru Ucraina, precum și cele mai recente evoluții ale războiului. Reuniunea de la Dublin este prima întâlnire la nivelul liderilor europeni dedicată exclusiv inteligenței artificiale (AI), potrivit Administrației Prezidențiale. La discuții vor participa și directorul general al companiei Mistral AI, Arthur Mensch, și profesorul Geoffrey Hinton, laureat al Premiului Nobel. Potrivit Administrației Prezidențiale, Nicușor Dan va susține necesitatea accelerării eforturilor Uniunii Europene pentru a rămâne competitivă în cursa globală pentru dezvoltarea inteligenței artificiale și pentru a evita apariția unor noi dependențe strategice. În acest context, președintele va pleda pentru consolidarea parteneriatelor cu Statele Unite, Canada și Japonia. Șeful statului va sublinia și importanța asigurării accesului companiilor europene și al administrațiilor publice la noile tehnologii, astfel încât aplicațiile bazate pe inteligență artificială să poată fi utilizate pe scară largă în industrie și economie, în toate statele membre. Citește și: Nicușor Dan, declarații după summitul de la Dublin: Am discutat de posibilitatea ca Germania să colaboreze la HUB-ul de la Marea Neagră Pentru atingerea acestui obiectiv este necesară mobilizarea capitalului public și privat, iar Fondul European de Competitivitate, prevăzut în viitorul buget al Uniunii, ar urma să joace un rol important. Nicușor Dan va atrage atenția și asupra implicațiilor pe care dezvoltarea inteligenței artificiale le poate avea asupra societății, inclusiv asupra pieței muncii, și asupra necesității pregătirii unor soluții pentru gestionarea acestor provocări. Un alt subiect important îl reprezintă utilizarea AI în atacuri cibernetice. Administrația Prezidențială avertizează că actori rău intenționați folosesc deja aceste tehnologii pentru a lansa astfel de atacuri, România numărându-se printre statele membre afectate. „În condiţiile în care aceste incidente sunt, în fapt, atacuri la adresa democraţiilor, preşedintele României va pleda pentru utilizarea la maximum a legislaţiei europene şi dezvoltarea cooperării cu partenerii internaţionali pentru a asigura utilizarea în siguranţă a AI la nivel global”, a transmis Administrația Prezidențială. Pe lângă inteligența artificială, liderii europeni vor discuta despre implicarea Uniunii Europene în negocierile de pace privind Ucraina și despre necesitatea transmiterii unui mesaj clar și unitar. Subiectul a fost adus în atenție de premierul Italiei, Giorgia Meloni, care a criticat, într-o scrisoare trimisă la 5 noiembrie, lipsa de coordonare a statelor membre în privința negocierilor de pace cu Rusia. Ca răspuns, președintele Consiliului European, Antonio Costa, i-a transmis că împărtășește opinia potrivit căreia Uniunea Europeană trebuie să participe la discuțiile care privesc securitatea continentului și viitorul Ucrainei. El a subliniat însă că această participare trebuie organizată astfel încât UE să își poată apăra interesele, să sprijine Ucraina și să transmită un mesaj comun. Liderii vor analiza și cele mai recente evoluții ale războiului, în special noua rundă de negocieri de pace desfășurată la Abu Dhabi, începută la 10 noiembrie 2026. Citește și: Nicușor Dan, întâlnire bilaterală cu Fridrich Merz, la Dublin. Ce au discutat președintele și cancelarul german La reuniunea informală de la Dublin vor participa liderii celor 27 de state membre, președinta Comisiei Europene, Ursula von der Leyen, și președintele Consiliului European, Antonio Costa, care va conduce lucrările. La discuțiile despre inteligența artificială, Arthur Mensch va prezenta perspectiva industriei asupra poziției Europei în competiția globală, precum și provocările strategice legate de competitivitate și suveranitate tehnologică. La rândul său, Geoffrey Hinton va aborda impactul mai larg al AI asupra societății, cu accent pe securitate și încredere, protejarea drepturilor fundamentale și a copiilor, funcționarea proceselor democratice, modelul social și riscurile de securitate cibernetică. Reuniunea informală are loc după summitul formal al Consiliului European din 15-16 octombrie, desfășurat la Bruxelles. Atunci, liderii au adoptat concluzii privind competitivitatea, sprijinul pentru Ucraina și Republica Moldova, viitorul buget multianual al UE, situația din Orientul Mijlociu, apărarea și securitatea europeană, migrația, extinderea Uniunii și reformele. Pe agenda reuniunii precedente s-au mai aflat securitatea regiunii arctice, situația din Ceuta și Melilla, protejarea spațiului digital, Conferința ONU privind schimbările climatice și jurisdicția internațională.
